Speculative decoding is a technique that accelerates text generation by leveraging the fact that large language models are often highly confident about the next few tokens. Instead of generating text one token at a time, which is slow because each step requires a full forward pass through the model, speculative decoding uses a smaller, faster "draft" model to predict a sequence of tokens. The main, larger model then evaluates this entire sequence in a single pass.

If the main model agrees with the draft model’s predictions, the entire sequence is accepted, and the process moves to the next chunk. This is a massive speedup because the expensive large model only performs one computation for multiple tokens. If the main model disagrees at any point, it rejects the draft from that point onward and generates the correct token itself, after which the process resumes.

The key insight is that this method does not change the output. The main model acts as the final arbiter. It only accepts tokens it would have generated anyway. If the draft model guesses wrong, the main model corrects it. Therefore, the final text is identical to what the main model would have produced if it had generated every token sequentially. The only difference is the speed at which it gets there.

This works because language models exhibit a "self-consistency" property: they are usually very confident about the next token, especially in predictable contexts. The draft model, being smaller and faster, can exploit this confidence to propose likely continuations. The main model’s role is simply to verify these proposals. By batching the verification of multiple tokens, speculative decoding reduces the number of expensive forward passes required, leading to significant latency improvements without sacrificing quality or altering the model’s intended output.

plain.content:
When a hash map receives a key, it runs that key through a hash function, which produces a number that gets reduced—usually by taking its remainder against the table size—to index into a fixed array. The trouble is that this function isn't one-to-one: two entirely different keys can land on the same index. That's a collision, and the language's implementation has to decide how to make room.

The most common approach is called chaining. Each slot in the underlying array doesn't hold a single key-value pair but rather points to a small collection of pairs, often a linked list or a small tree. When a collision occurs, the new entry is simply appended to that slot's list. Lookups stay cheap as long as each bucket stays short; the hash function is doing its job if the keys are well-distributed. A second common strategy, called open addressing, avoids lists altogether. If the target slot is occupied, the probe sequence walks to neighboring slots—next slot, next-plus-two, next-plus-four, or a secondary hash-derived offset—until an empty slot is found. The entry is stored there, and a lookup that hits an occupied slot must follow the same probe sequence to confirm whether the desired key is present or whether the slot was never actually filled for that key. Chaining tends to be simpler and handles deletions cleanly, while open addressing often has better cache behavior because it keeps everything in one contiguous array, but it's sensitive to how the probe sequence is chosen.

Both strategies keep performance reasonable only up to a point. As more entries are added, buckets get longer (in chaining) or empty slots become harder to find (in open addressing), and the constant hiding inside the "average O(1)" lookup quietly inflates toward O(n). To prevent that, the map tracks a ratio called the load factor—the number of entries divided by the table's capacity. When the load factor crosses a threshold, commonly somewhere around 0.7 for chaining-based maps, the implementation triggers a resize. It allocates a new, larger backing array, almost always double the old size, so that the load factor drops back well below the threshold. Every existing entry is then reinserted into the new array: each key is re-hashed, and its new index is computed against the new, larger modulus. Because the hash function's output is now being taken modulo a different number, the entries scatter across a wider range of slots, and the average bucket length or probe length shrinks again.

The resize itself is an O(n) operation—every key gets a fresh hash computed and a fresh position placed—but it happens rarely enough that the cost is spread over many subsequent insertions. If the map grows by a factor of two each time, the total work of all resizes over n insertions is proportional to n, not n squared, which is what makes the overall insertion cost amortize to a constant. In practice you'll notice the resize as a small pause after a particular insert, after which the table feels fast again for a while. Some implementations also resize when deletions drive the load factor too low, shrinking the table to reclaim memory, though that policy varies by library.

plain.content:
A hash map stores key-value pairs by first running the key through a hash function, which produces an integer that indexes into an internal array of fixed size. Two distinct keys, however, can produce the same integer, and when that happens we call it a collision. There are two broad strategies for dealing with this, and most implementations pick one or a variant of it.

The first approach is called chaining. Each slot in the array holds a small linked list (or similar small collection) of entries. When a key hashes to a slot, you simply append the entry to that list, so a slot can hold many entries with the same hash value. Lookups and insertions first jump to the right slot, then walk the list to find or add the matching key. This keeps insertions fast regardless of how many collisions pile up in a given slot, though in the pathological case where every key hashes to the same bucket, operations degrade to scanning the entire list.

The second approach is open addressing. Every entry lives directly in the array; there are no separate lists. When a collision is detected—meaning the computed slot is already occupied—the implementation probes the array for the next available slot using a deterministic pattern, such as linear probing (checking slot, slot+1, slot+2, and so on), quadratic probing (offsets that grow quadratically), or double hashing (two hash functions combined to determine the step size). You keep probing until you find an empty slot, place the entry there, and remember the rule so that future lookups can trace the same path. The tradeoff here is that deletions become trickier, because simply clearing a slot can break the probe chain for later entries, so implementations use a "tombstone" marker instead.

As entries are added, the table fills up and performance begins to suffer. For chaining, long lists mean more comparisons per lookup. For open addressing, a dense table means probes take many steps and cluster, and eventually a slot might be occupied forever, making insertion impossible. To keep things healthy, the hash map tracks a metric called the load factor, which is essentially the ratio of stored entries to the number of slots in the table. When that ratio crosses a threshold chosen by the implementation—commonly somewhere around 0.7 for open addressing tables—the map decides it's time to resize.

Resizing means allocating a new, larger array (typically double the previous size) and reinserting every existing key-value pair into it. Each key goes through the hash function again to find its slot in the new table, so the same collision behavior is recomputed from scratch. In practice, the new table is more spread out, so the load factor drops and the average number of comparisons or probe steps per operation goes back down. For chaining, the entries are simply redistributed across the larger number of slots. The operation itself is somewhat expensive because every entry must be touched, which is why it's amortized over many inserts rather than paying the full cost on every single one. Some implementations also shrink the table when deletions drive the load factor well below a lower threshold, to avoid holding onto more memory than necessary.

A hash map stores key-value pairs by first running the key through a hash function, which turns the key into a numeric index that points to a particular slot in an internal array. The problem, of course, is that two different keys can produce the same numeric index — a collision. There are two mainstream strategies for dealing with this. When a collision happens, the new entry is simply appended to that list, so many keys can share the same index without overwriting one another. Most well-known implementations, like Java's HashMap or Python's dict, use chaining, with a small tree-like structure kicked in for long chains.

When that ratio crosses a threshold (a common choice, like three-quarters for Java's HashMap, meaning 75% of the slots are in use), the map decides it is time to resize. It allocates a new array, typically twice as large, and then rehashes every single entry, recomputing each key's index and placing it into the new array. Without this growth, a hash map filled to capacity would see its chaining lists or open-addressing probes get longer and longer, and the average lookup time that is normally a constant would degrade toward linear in the number of elements. A hash map works by turning a key into a number (a hash value) and using that number to pick a slot in an underlying array. The catch is that different keys can produce the same number. When that happens, two or more entries are competing for the same slot, and this is called a collision.

Most hash maps deal with collisions in one of two main ways. The first is called chaining, or sometimes separate chaining. In this scheme, each slot in the array doesn't hold a single key-value pair; it holds the head of a small linked list (or similar sequence) of entries that happen to share that slot. To find a value, the map computes the hash, jumps to the slot, and then walks through the entries in that slot's list, comparing keys until it finds a match. Insertion works the same way — you just tack the new pair onto the end of that slot's list. Chaining is forgiving: even a terrible hash function where everything collides into one slot will still work, it just degenerates into a slow linked-list scan.

The second approach, called open addressing, avoids lists entirely. Instead of putting multiple items in one slot, the map probes nearby slots using a deterministic rule — linear probing (try the next slot), quadratic probing, double hashing, and so on — until it finds an empty one. This keeps everything in a flat array, which is friendlier to CPU caches, but it does create a subtle problem called clustering: if a slot is occupied, it nudges the next item a position over, which nudges the one after it, and so on. A long contiguous run of filled slots slows down lookups because the probe sequence gets longer.

Either way, collisions are tolerable as long as they're rare. The map tracks how full the array is using a metric called the load factor, which is essentially the number of stored entries divided by the number of slots. When the load factor crosses a threshold — typically somewhere around 0.7 to 0.8, depending on the implementation — performance degrades noticeably: chains get long or probe sequences get long, and every lookup or insert that used to be a quick constant-time hit now takes longer.

That's the trigger for resizing. The map allocates a larger array (commonly twice the current capacity), computes a new hash for every existing key (using the larger array's size, which changes the modulo arithmetic), and scatters all entries into their new slots. This rehashing pass is where the temporary O(n) cost lives; without it, the table would fill up and the collision penalty would keep growing. In many implementations, the resize is lazy: the map only rehashes when a load that would push the factor over the threshold actually occurs, rather than checking after every single operation. After the resize the load factor drops back down toward zero, the table has breathing room again, and the next round of inserts can proceed before hitting the threshold once more.

A well-behaved hash map thus quietly manages itself: it tolerates the inevitable collisions with a cheap strategy (a list or a probe), monitors how crowded things are, and when congestion becomes the rule rather than the exception, it quietly pays the one-time cost of moving everything into a bigger home.

plain.content:
When two different keys hash to the same slot in a hash map's internal array, we call that a collision, and the map has to figure out where to actually store the new entry. There are two broad strategies. In one, called chaining, each slot in the array holds a small linked list, and every key that hashes to that slot is appended to the list. To find a value you first hash the key to get the slot, then walk down that little list comparing keys until you find the match or reach the end. This is the classic textbook approach and it is what Java's HashMap uses (though Java also switches a bucket from a linked list to a balanced tree if the list gets very long, to guard against adversarial input). The other strategy, called open addressing, keeps the array free of extra bookkeeping. When the hash points to an already-occupied slot, the map doesn't just stop; instead it probes a second slot, a third, and so on, using a deterministic offset function (linear probing tries slot + 1, slot + 2, slot + 3; double hashing uses a second independent hash to pick the stride). It keeps probing until it finds an empty slot, and it stores the key there. To retrieve the value later it must replay that exact same probe sequence until it finds the key or hits an empty slot, which is why deleting in an open-addressing table requires a subtle tombstone marker so you don't prematurely "stop looking." Python's dictionary uses open addressing, as does C++'s unordered_map.

The reason a hash map has to resize at all is that both strategies degrade in performance as the table fills up. In the chaining world, the average length of each little linked list grows in proportion to how full the table is; in the open-addressing world, the expected number of probes grows much faster than linearly as the table approaches fullness, and if you ever let it fill completely you can end up probing forever. The map therefore tracks a load factor, which is simply the number of stored entries divided by the capacity of the array. Each implementation picks a threshold—0.75 is the traditional Java choice, many open-addressing implementations sit around 0.5 to 0.75 to leave generous room—and whenever a single insert pushes the load factor above that threshold, a resize is triggered. The resize works by allocating a larger array (almost always double the old size, sometimes 3/2 or some other factor), iterating over every key-value pair in the old table, recomputing each key's hash and placing it into the new array with the same collision-resolution procedure, and then discarding the old array. That rehashing pass takes O(n) time in the number of entries, so a single insert that triggers a resize is itself O(n), but across a long sequence of inserts the total work spent on all resizes adds up to only O(n) overall (a geometric series), which is what makes the amortized cost of each operation effectively O(1).

Some maps also shrink. If you repeatedly delete entries until the table becomes mostly empty, the load factor falls well below a lower threshold, and a well-behaved implementation will halve the array to reclaim memory. Shrinkage is less common than growth because the cost of rehashing everything into a smaller table is the same and there is less of a memory-saving benefit, but the principle is the same: keep the load factor inside a comfortable band so that neither lookup nor insert has to scan a disproportionately long chain or probe sequence.
